card: Hegel's diligence from Brunswick, carrying him and a 25- or 26-year-old Englishman bound from Italy for Paris, reached Northeim at 3 pm the previous day. As it would wait there until 8 or 9 pm, Hegel hired a post-chaise through Göttingen to Münden, arriving at 10 pm; after sleeping until 6 am he went on to Kassel.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I arrive in Kassel, weary but intact. The diligence from Brunswick was a misadventure; stuck in Northeim until the evening, I hired a post-chaise through Göttingen to Münden, arriving at ten. I slept until six, then continued here. My fellow traveler, a young Englishman of twenty-five returning from Italy to Paris, is loud, ill-dressed, and speaks of “the sublime” with a vulgarity that makes one’s teeth ache. He is a man without a state, purely accidental.

The food was tolerable, the wine thin. I have paid the driver his due. I think of you and the boys, but mostly I think of the mud on my boots. Tell Karl his father is still alive, if that is of any comfort to him. I shall continue tomorrow.

Yours,
G.W.F.
Y: After having slept through the afternoon; though before that I had seen beautiful gardens, an iron obelisk—70 feet high—erected in memory of the two last Dukes who perished in the war against the French, and in the evening I had seen a bad comedy, we set out again after 10 o’clock on the diligence (though more, according to Wolff’s travesty, on the sloth). The night was beautiful, the stars shone magnificently, — the morning star rose particularly beautifully. Now in the daytime we saw a different physiognomy of nature than before, no longer the barren or fertile plains, — beautiful oak forests, mountains, hills, the gentle slopes covered with fruit fields, the valleys filled with meadows, — in short a homely nature — homely, namely for me, for you yourself, born in half-sand, are in Berlin in the homely element, perhaps in a slightly stronger dose. — So in such a beautiful land we traveled on. With my Englishman, who speaks French, and also some German, I got along very well, he is a young man of 25–26 years, a handsome man, somewhat like the actor Blum, and of such, but better, bearing, good-natured, well-informed, comes from Italy, is going to Paris, to travel from there via Milan to Constantinople, a private person, not too rich — in short as I would also wish for companions in the future. In Nordheim, where we arrived at 3 o’clock in the afternoon (yesterday Wednesday), and the carriage had to wait until about 8 or 9 o’clock in the evening for another, I considered that it would be too uncomfortable for me to spend the third night without a bed and proper sleep; I therefore took extra post — it went first to Göttingen — the scholarly Göttingen; say however only to the dear friend Schulze, that as a proper Berlin professor I did not make much of it, to drive on in 5 minutes, but I did not shake the dust from my feet outside the gate, only because I had not picked any up with them. So I traveled to Münden, where I arrived at 10 o’clock — and slept quietly in bed until 6 o’clock today — and finally here. The road is very charming, Cassel lies very excellently in a wide valley; — the Hercules on Wilhelmshöhe is already visible from several hours away as a peak in the middle of a mountain range. Around Cassel itself it is very beautiful; it has streets — i.e. in one part — in the style of Berlin; the Aue is a layout of approximately the kind of the new garden in Potsdam, beautiful green lawn with healthy varied trees scattered, without any shrubbery, — so transparent everywhere; — it is most charming to walk in it — at the end a beautiful water surface, with hanging willows here and there lining the bank, benches etc., also a house where one can drink coffee in the open air, coffee, i.e. chicory broth; for many days I have only had such, and no coffee to drink, — the whole Brunswick country is covered with fields of this lying root. Tomorrow I will go up to Wilhelmshöhe and into the gallery; today the Englishman has left me in the lurch....

card: Hegel moved out of the Hôtel des Princes in the morning and left his belongings for the time being at Cousin's; the two meant to find a furnished room (chambre garnie) that morning. At 11 they ate a short breakfast of cutlets with a bottle of wine, as Cousin was to get Hegel's letter to the post by 2.
X: This morning I moved out of the Hotel des Princes and provisionally left the effects with my friend Cousin—it is very expensive there—this morning we will find a furnished room. That we are well together, in heartfelt cordiality, goes without saying—we did not linger long at breakfast (i.e., at 11 o'clock we ate cutlets and drank a bottle of wine) because he has to look after the interests of Mrs. Hegel, i.e., to see to it that this letter gets to the post office today, which must be by 2 o'clock...
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The heat in Paris is oppressive, though the air is thick with the scent of frying onions from the street stalls. This morning we moved out of the Hôtel des Princes, leaving our baggage at Cousin’s, a man of great intellect but little practical sense. We spent the hours hunting for a *chambre garnie*, a task more tedious than deciphering the *Geist*. Finally, at 11, we settled for a modest room near the Seine. Cousin insisted on a brief breakfast: cutlets, decent but heavy, and a bottle of good Burgundy. He is frantic to get my letter to the post by two, fearing the mail coaches have already departed.

I am tired. The dust here is worse than in the Rhineland. Tell the boys to mind their conduct; I expect them to be orderly, not merely happy.

Your husband,
G.W.F.

card: Having come from Breda the day before via Moerdijk, a steamboat crossing of the Hollandsch Diep, Dordrecht, Rotterdam and Delft, Hegel went in the morning through the woods to Scheveningen, an hour away, and saw the North Sea. He then visited the picture gallery, walked in the Bois in the afternoon, and in the evening saw three French comedies.
X: From Breda I continued on by diligence at 10 o’clock in the morning, for three run daily from Antwerp to Amsterdam, all via The Hague, and likewise three in return; — from Brussels to Paris, diligences also run every day, one is in Paris in 36 hours for 25 francs, what a temptation! had it not been so late in the season, and besides — had I had news from you, — could one have resisted such a temptation? Likewise in Rotterdam, here a steamboat goes once a week to London — punctual and infallible, unless there is very bad storm — in 24 hours. But now from Breda it went on yesterday without a break, — fertile land, but entirely now on brick-paved roads, like the sidewalk in Berlin — to Mordyk, from there by steamboat across a bay of the sea, the Holland Diep, 1/2 hour wide — my dear friend, the southwest, which had brought me such fine weather for so long, also helped with the better crossing; here ships came from afar, a proud three-masted ship, like a Sultan: majestic white turban, equally swollen white middle garment, then a white, wider lower garment, and a cloak behind, as the figure shows?). From here to Dordrecht, — large seaport, forty, or God knows how many thousand inhabitants; — from here in true Holland, — all houses of reddish bricks, with white lines as if made with a ruler, no edge, no corner crumbled or blunted, — beautiful canals, planted with trees, running through the city, everything full of large ships, the straight beautiful quays everywhere; — then again after 3 o’clock across the wide Meuse; then at 5 o’clock in Rotterdam; what a large city again! then through Delft and after half an hour into beautiful The Hague. The Hague is in fact a village — everywhere beautiful green meadows, so from Dordrecht on! The cleanest vegetable gardens, as nicely kept as Mrs. Voß can keep them, interrupted by rows of trees and cut off from the highway, next to which a canal always runs, and from each other, — cattle everywhere on them, — all black- and white-spotted, they also stay on the meadow at night, one sees people in the evening milking the cows; one travels among all the Potters and Berghems. — This morning out of the gate into a forest, like the Berlin Zoo, only more beautiful alleys of beeches and oaks, no undergrowth — all high and leafy forest; — one hour to Scheveningen, here I saw the unbounded North Sea, the German Sea — my friend the southwest blew strongly and brought the most beautiful waves. — Then I saw the gallery, afternoon strolled in the beautiful woods, more beautiful than the Aue near Cassel, splendid water pieces like in Charlottenburg; — then also once a French comedy and indeed three in one evening seen; I had to rest, for I have walked and stood a lot; — in the gallery is a Württemberg inspector, — beautiful, very beautiful things. — I have today before the mirror tied my neckerchief and seen that I, as I believe, have become thinner, for I have had many fatigues, — but I am otherwise healthy and vigorous and well; also with the money it is still going well, — I have lost, I believe, also nothing yet, and I am almost annoyed about it, for in something one must have bad luck, — but I calculate that I pay for everything in that I have no letters from you
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The sea at Scheveningen is a flat, grey nothing. I walked an hour through the woods to see it and found only damp sand and the smell of fish. A waste of boots, truly. The picture gallery here is decent, though the light in the afternoon was poor. I paid two guilders for a decent dinner in Delft earlier, which was reasonable.

I sat in the Bois for an hour, watching the Dutch look at me with that peculiar, polite indifference. They are a people of water and trade, lacking that fiery spirit of the South, but they have their order. In the evening, three French comedies. The first was tiresome, the second decent, the third a farce of the lowest kind. I laughed, but mostly from relief that it was over.

Karl writes that his Latin is improving. I hope his discipline holds. Do not worry about the cold; I have brought my best coat. I shall return to Berlin soon.

Your loving,
G.W.F. Hegel

card: In Amsterdam Hegel posted his letter, saw the second part of the picture gallery and the former town hall, which Napoleon had made an imperial palace and the royal family occupies when in the city. He visited a church noted for its coloured windows, lunched on fish with Dr. Besseling, a Catholic, and left by diligence at 5 pm.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The fish at Besseling’s table was tolerable, if a bit too white for my taste, and the Dutch wine was warm. I paid three guilders for the pleasure, which I find exorbitant for such a meal. Dr. Besseling is a pleasant enough Catholic, though he spoke of the Pope with a reverence I found rather theatrical. I have left Amsterdam for Utrecht by diligence, arriving as the light fails.

I saw the former town hall here, now the imperial palace. It is a grand building, though one cannot help but feel a certain melancholy seeing the scars of Napoleon’s ambition still lingering on the walls. The coloured windows in the church were indeed striking; the light through them had a quality that almost made the stone feel alive. I am tired, my love. The journey has been long and the roads are not as smooth as one hopes. I hope the boys are well and that you have not had any trouble with the household accounts. I shall write again when I can find a quiet hour.

Yours,
G.W.F.
Y: So far, I am happy; my last letter from Amsterdam will be in your hands, my dear! I sent it off early on Saturday, on which day I also saw the second, most varied part of the picture gallery—wonderful pieces among them—and further the former town hall, which Napoleon had had set up as an imperial palace. Setting aside this division of rooms and the furnishings, etc., the building (which the royal family still inhabits when they are in Amsterdam) is the most magnificent conception of a town house that a free, wealthy, art-loving citizenry could have conceived. After visiting a church famous for its colored windows and having lunch with Mr. D. Besseling, at whose place I, because he is a stricter Catholic than my Mr. van Ghert, ate fish both times, but excellent fish, I got on the diligence at 5 o’clock in the evening (on Saturday).

card: Hegel stopped for the night at Duxan, which lies a little more than halfway along the road from Prague to Töplitz.
X: You probably hardly know where Duxan is in the world; I myself have only known it for half an hour; I will share my knowledge with you as well. Duxan lies a little more than halfway on the road from Prague to Töplitz, and I am spending the night here.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The carriage rattled us to Duxan by four, half-way to Töplitz. The innkeeper, a stout Bohemian named Kral, insisted we stay, citing the mist closing in over the Elbe. He was right; the view from the window is grey and flat, a perfect mirror of my mood after eating cold mutton. The wine is thin, but the snuff is excellent. I paid three florins for the room and dinner; a fair price for the dust.

Karl’s letter reached me in Prague. I see he has begun his studies. Tell him to listen to his instructors, not his own cleverness. Obedience is the soil in which judgment grows. Do not let Ludwig linger too long at the café; I want him walking with me tomorrow.

The mist is thickening. I will sleep soon. Kiss the boys for me.

Your
G.W.F.

card: Hegel arrived in Paris on Sunday between 10 and 11, took a room at the Hôtel des Princes and at once sought out Cousin. He saw from outside the Boulevards, Palais Royal, Louvre, Tuileries and Luxembourg. That evening he went to the Champs Élysées, with its carousel and cafés such as the Ambassadeurs and the Aurore, crowded with families.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I am settled at the Hôtel des Princes, a decent enough room for the price, though the air is thick. I saw Cousin this evening; he is still chattering about "spirit" as if he had invented it, which is amusing given our own work. We walked the Boulevards later. The Palais Royal is a labyrinth of small shops, and the Tuileries were quiet. But the Champs Élysées! It is a spectacle. The Ambassadeurs and Aurore are packed with families, children spinning on carousels, coffee being drunk in great quantities. It feels less like a city and more like a large, noisy market for the soul.

The food here is light; I ate a simple soup and some bread, perhaps too little. I am tired. The journey from Berlin has worn me down. I miss the stillness of our house and the sound of the boys’ voices. I shall rest now. Do not worry; I am well, just far away.

Your loving Georg
Y: Here, between 10 and 11 o'clock on Sunday, having arrived yesterday, I took up quarters at the Hôtel des Princes, — and immediately sought out my cousin. — But here I am overwhelmed by the multitude of great sights I have already seen and traversed, that is to say, from the outside. The Boulevards, the Palais Royal, the Louvre, the Tuileries, the Luxembourg, the Garden and Palace, and so on. — Last evening the Champs Elysées, where the Carousel is, and the taverns, that is to say, the coffee houses, namely those of the Ambassadeur and of the Aurore, — a state of affairs like at the tents, — only ten times more people at the tables, philistines with wives and children, and so forth. — When I walk through the streets, the people look exactly as they do in Berlin, — all dressed in the same way, roughly the same faces, — the same appearance, but in a populous mass.

card: Hegel arrived in Hamburg by ship about 10 am and had his luggage sent to the post office for that day's express coach, to be home by Monday. No seat was free, even for Wednesday; two letters from Marie were waiting. He was at the König von Hannover inn; the next possible departure was Monday's post wagon, arriving Thursday.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I arrived in Hamburg at ten this morning. The heat was oppressive, and the boat ride from Cuxhaven felt less like travel and more like being marinated in brine. I found no passage for today’s express coach, nor even for Wednesday. I am lodged at the König von Hannover, a tolerable house, though the rooms are damp and the beer tastes of tar.

Your two letters waited for me at the post office. I read them by the window, watching the cranes load timber. I was relieved to hear of Karl’s progress, though I suspect Immanuel is still resisting the arithmetic. I must stay here until Monday’s post wagon, arriving Thursday. It is a long wait, but I shall not complain. The city is busy, the air thick, and I have already spent three thalers on a lunch that was barely worth the effort.

I miss your snuff and your sharp tongue. Write when you can.

Yours,
G.W.F.
Y: I have just arrived, and am having my things sent from the ship to the post office, in order to catch the express post today and be with you on Monday; — there is no more space available, not even on Wednesday, but as compensation I find two dear letters from you; how relieved and delighted I am by these good news from you.... I am sitting here in the King of Hanover — before the most beautiful view. — But now I can only depart on Monday by the post coach, which has given me a sense of apprehension, and will not arrive until Thursday.

card: Hegel visited the greenhouses by the Burg, entering and leaving through a kind of underground passage which the Emperor uses every day when he spends some afternoon hours in his gardens.
X: Greenhouses by the Castle, went in and out through a kind of underground passage, through which the Emperor goes every day, and spends some afternoon hours in his gardens. — But the bloom — I could only hope for georginas and altheas — quite insignificant, — that is quite different on the Peacock Island.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The air in the Burg greenhouses is thick with the scent of orange blossoms, a sharp contrast to the stale study air in Berlin. I walked the Emperor’s private path today, entering through an underground passage he uses for his afternoon retreats. It is a curious thing, to walk in the footsteps of absolute power while smelling damp earth and rotting fruit. I paid six kreuzer for a bottle of water and a small cake, which was dry and tasteless.

I met a young professor from Prague, eager to discuss Fries. I told him plainly that his system is a house of cards; he looked pale, then left. I am tired from the walk and the heat. The light here is yellow, unlike our clear blue. I hope Karl’s health is steady. I shall write again from Brno. Give my regards to Immanuel.

Yours,
G.W.F.

card: Hegel reached Magdeburg at 1 pm. The next coach to Kassel left on Tuesday noon. That afternoon he saw the cathedral, with cast apostles by Fischer of Nuremberg, called on General Carnot, and walked by the Elbe as 13 Hamburg ships sailed in. Next morning a coachman due to drive an Englishman to Kassel in three days arrived.
X: The first thing I would have to tell you for a good morning, namely that we arrived here safely, partly follows from this itself; the company were decent people; it got cold at night; yet four woolen body linings or skirts protected me sufficiently, so that I, after having with difficulty peeled myself off again, have remained unharmed. Yesterday at noon at 1 o'clock we arrived here, but it is harder to get out of Magdeburg than to come in. — The activity of Mr. Post President and the Prussian intelligence have not yet cast their eye on the local post coach business, at least insofar as it concerns my interest. Until Tuesday noon only does the — I almost said — coach to Cassel go. The journaliers with which I came is not connected with any further courses. To stay here until Tuesday is far too long. So I resolved first, since tomorrow morning the traveling coach to Erfurt goes, to take my course thither; how nice, to bring Goethe the package, which I would have to send from here, myself and from there to go on along the great highway! — Thereupon I looked at the post coach, but what a cart! and then I would have to drive about 44 miles to Cassel — so I decided to take extra post, but I have to hear that I would be carried on further on the same cart, wagon, under open sky. With this briefly resolved, to return quickly to Berlin and to fetch my traveling coach, and with this well equipped, to pleasantly continue my health journey. With this cheerful thought, to see you dear ones again soon, I then fell asleep and slept very well; yet, you see, not, like Peter, in the sense of staying at home, but on the contrary to travel out thoroughly. The former would otherwise have been no wonder either, for I indeed went on the journey with greater reluctance than I dared to say, and if I had not already received the money, it would have been hard to bring me to it, so necessary it was to me in fact. Besides, I also yesterday afternoon saw what there was to see here; — the famous cathedral — it may be remarkable, because it is a cathedral; — but the whole architecture is not such a good conception as the Nuremberg Gothic churches, and what of artwork is inside, a lot of carved and cast, painted and plastered, is far too bad. The cast apostles by Fischer, the Nuremberger, are not to be compared with the Nurembergers. The subjects have entirely fallen into the craft! The dearest thing I have seen is General Carnot, a lovable old man and Frenchman; it is the famous one; — he took it friendly that I visited him. — Then I strolled on the Elbe, a fleet of 13 Hamburg ships with high-swollen sea sails was coming in (each with two, yet only on one mast), beautiful stream, beautiful immeasurable fertile plains (here fertile, but otherwise between Potsdam and Burg, what we saw by day, quite desolate) — more beautiful the clearest sky. Just now a coachman comes, who has to bring an Englishman, who seems to be a German, to Cassel in 3 days; to him I will attach myself...
Y:
My dearest Marie,

I reached Magdeburg at one this afternoon. The heat is oppressive, but I managed a walk by the Elbe. Thirteen Hamburg ships came in; the sight was grand, though the dockworkers were rough. I visited the cathedral to see the cast apostles by Fischer of Nuremberg. They are stiff, lifeless things—nature forced into bronze without breath. I also called on General Carnot. He is a polite man, but his conversation was dry as old bread. We drank wine, decent enough, and I paid two thalers for the meal.

I am told the coach to Kassel leaves Tuesday noon. A coachman arrived this morning to drive an Englishman there in three days; he seems hurried. I hope you and the boys are well. I missed our cards last night. The air is thick here, and my head is heavy. I will write again when I am settled.

Your affectionate
G.W.F. Hegel

card: After Hegel returned from an excursion, Cousin handed him a letter from Marie in which she wrote about his illness and her worries over it; his son Immanuel had also written, asking what had made him ill.
X:
My dearest Marie,

You write of my illness with such alarm, and Immanuel asks what caused it? It was merely the damp cold and a bad digestion, nothing more. I am well now.

I spent the morning with Cousin. He is a clever man, though he talks too much about "spirit" without having read the *Phenomenology*. He insisted on paying for my dinner at the Café de Paris—four francs for a mediocre soup and a glass of claret. I let him, as it is a fine way to settle accounts. The wine was ordinary, but the company was livelier than usual.

I walked the Tuileries in the late afternoon. The light on the Seine was quite beautiful, but the crowds are thick with tourists. I bought a small snuff box for two francs to replace the one I lost in Berlin.

I am not ill, only tired. Tell Karl to stop worrying so much, or he will be the next one to fall.

Your loving husband,
G.W.F.
Y: After returning from this excursion, Cousin gave me your kind letter, in which you write to me about my ill health and your worries about it. Immanuel writes, what caused me to become unwell? — he must know that I am no longer such a small springing-about fellow as he, but already an old father, — that I wish for advanced age and health, especially in order to see him and his brother continue to flourish, and to be able to contribute my part to it, — and to be able to share with you, my dear, for a long time yet, this satisfaction which is to be hoped for and which was brought into fresher remembrance on his birthday...

card: The weather was bad on Sunday afternoon. Having overlooked the unusual starting time on the playbill, Hegel reached the theatre only at 7 and missed the chorus 'Es lebe unser guter Kaiser Franz'. He then heard the first act of Zelmira, with Dardanelli, Donzelli and Lablache; Donzelli sang a recitative.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The weather turned foul on Sunday, and I, in my usual haste, overlooked the early start at the Hofoper. I arrived at seven, far too late for the opening chorus in praise of Franz. A minor tragedy, but I made the best of it. We heard the first act of *Zelmira*. Dardanelli was decent, but Lablache was a bore. Donzelli, however, sang a recitative that was quite exquisite—pure, clear, and without affectation. I paid six florins for a good seat, which I consider fair for the evening’s entertainment.

The food at the theatre was mediocre, as usual, so I dined on simple soup and bread. I think of you and the boys, and the quiet of our home in Berlin. The noise here is tiresome.

Yours,
G.W.F. Hegel
Y: Bad weather on Sunday afternoon. — Because I overlooked the note on the theater program: “Start exceptionally /67 o’clock,” I only went at 7 o’clock and just missed the main thing: the chorus “Long live our good Emperor Franz”; — then the first act of Zelmira, how Dardanelli sang divinely! and above all Donzelli a recitative, which was his triumph! in opera seria he is unsurpassed, — he and Lablache — bearded with black curls, what antique heads!

card: Hegel and his party went to the English company at the Odeon, near where he lodged, rather than hear Pesaroni, who sang that evening. He had earlier seen Mlle Mars in Emilia, the only piece she was then appearing in.
X: I have not been to the French theatre as much as I had thought; the small theatres and plays are pleasant, but I am soon done with them; they are jokes that one quickly gets over. Mlle Mars is currently playing only in *Emilia*, in which I saw her. The Pesaroni sang yesterday, but we preferred the English, who are in my neighbourhood (Odeon).
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The English company at the Odeon was a necessary refuge. Pesaroni sings, but tonight the air here demanded something else, and the theatre near my lodgings obliged. The actors were adequate; the scenery, as usual in Paris, a bit of painted cardboard. I paid two francs for a seat that smelled of damp wool.

We saw Mlle Mars earlier in *Emilia*. She is still formidable, though her voice has thinned. It is interesting to watch how the public swallows her gestures as if they were logical proofs. One sees the spirit of the age in their applause.

I am well. The wine in the Rhineland was better than anything I have found here. Do tell the boys to mind their conduct at the Gymnasium; obedience is the only foundation that holds.

I shall sleep late tomorrow.

Yours ever,
G.W.F. Hegel

card: After lunch Hegel went back to the post office in Kassel and booked a seat on the next day's diligence to Giessen, where the road to Koblenz leaves the Frankfurt road. While there he received a letter from his wife Marie.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I have secured a seat on the diligence for tomorrow, departing Kassel at six to Giessen, where the road splits for Koblenz. The heat here is oppressive; I paid three Kreuzers for a bottle of water at the post office, which felt like robbery, though the clerk was polite enough. I have been walking the streets to cool off. The town is neat but lacks the grandeur of Berlin. I saw a group of students playing whist in a tavern; their form was poor, but their enthusiasm was loud.

Regarding your last letter: I am well, though my shoes are wearing thin. I think of Karl and Immanuel often. The journey is tiring, but the view from the window is pleasant. Do not worry about my health. I will write again when I reach Giessen.

Yours,
G.W.F.
Y: When I went to the post office again after dinner today, where I also registered for tomorrow’s diligence to Giessen—from there the road branches off from the Frankfurt road toward Coblenz—I received your letter, my dear, and cannot tell you enough what joy it gave me.

card: After the Prater, Hegel went to the Leopoldstadt theatre. A prelude was given in which Schuster played an elderly merchant with a young wife, followed once more by Die Zauberbirn.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The air in Vienna is thick with the smell of roasted chestnuts and indifference. We spent the afternoon in the Prater; the crowds were immense, but the rides were dull. I paid two Gulden for a carriage that shook my teeth loose.

Dinner was late, at the old tavern near the Ring. The soup was cold, but the wine was a decent Zweigelt. I met Schuster afterward. He is a large man, loud as a trumpet, and claims his new role in *Die Zauberbirn* makes him the king of the stage. I suspect he is merely the loudest. I attended the performance tonight. The prelude was tedious, but Schuster’s merchant was surprisingly alive. The young wife, however, looked as if she wished to be anywhere else.

I miss the quiet of our study. The heat here makes thinking difficult. I have bought a new coat; the tailor overcharged me, but the fabric is fine.

Yours,
G.W.F.
Y: After the Prater, to the Leopoldstadt Theatre; here a prelude, in which Schuster, almost in the same manner as the older merchant with a young woman, as before, and then once again the Magic Pear; if only I could have had the young ones with me, — you yourself would not have been too old to amuse yourself a second time with it, as was my case.

card: Hegel left by express post at 4 the previous morning and reached Trier, over 16 German miles away, at 8. On 28 August, from after 8 until 1:30, a brother of the innkeeper showed him the Roman ruins and the surrounding area, including an estate of the brother-in-law of Procurator-General Eichhorn. In the afternoon Hegel visited the churches.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I am exhausted, having driven sixteen German miles from the previous night’s post to reach Trier by eight this morning. The heat was stifling. From eight until half-past one, the innkeeper’s brother, a man of little conversation but decent company, showed me the Roman ruins and the surrounding countryside. We visited an estate belonging to the Procurator-General Eichhorn’s brother-in-law; the grounds are respectable, though the house itself is merely adequate. I dined on a heavy local fare and paid a reasonable sum, though the wine was slightly acidic.

In the afternoon, I walked the churches. The stone here bears the weight of centuries, a silent witness to the progress of consciousness, though I suspect you would find my weariness more interesting than my musings on masonry. I have no news for the boys save that I am well and eating sufficiently.

I must rest. The journey continues tomorrow.

Your affectionate husband,
G.W.F.
Y: Yesterday I had to get up at 3 o’clock in the morning in order to depart precisely at 4 o’clock by the express post for here; the journey is over 16 miles, very frequently just up hill, down hill, but on a fine carriage road; at 8 o’clock we were here. — I find everywhere people whom I know, and who are otherwise obliging and friendly. After I had slept well, I set out on my way after 8 o’clock, under the guidance of a brother of the innkeeper, who showed me the remarkable Roman ruins and took me around the area, among other things to an estate of the brother-in-law of the General Prosecutor Eichhorn; we were on our feet until 11½ o’clock. — Trier has an excellent location on the Moselle, a beautiful valley of the greatest fertility, bounded by gentle vineyards. — In the afternoon I was in the churches.

card: Hegel reached Weimar at sunset on 16 October and went to Goethe, where Riemer and Zelter were present. The Grand Duke came to tea half an hour later; Hegel sat beside him on the sofa and they conversed until 9:30. At 10 the next morning Hegel and Zelter drove in Goethe's carriage to the Grand Duke's botanical garden at Belvedere.
X:
My dearest Marie,

We arrived in Weimar at sunset, and I was straight away at Goethe’s. Riemer and Zelter were there, and the Grand Duke joined us for tea half an hour later. We sat together on the sofa and talked until nearly ten. It was a pleasant evening, though I confess my back aches from the carriage ride.

This morning, Zelter and I took Goethe’s carriage to the Grand Duke’s botanical garden at Belvedere. The collection is impressive, though the light was rather harsh for my eyes. We ate a simple lunch; the bread was good, the wine mediocre, and I paid six thalers for the pleasure. Goethe is still sharp, if a bit tired. The Grand Duke is affable but speaks in circles. I hope this letter finds you and the boys well. I have little else to report.

Your husband,
G.W.F. Hegel
Y: My last letter had brought me as far as Elberfeld; from there it went straight across Westphalia via Arnsberg and Arolsen to Kassel. From Arnsberg, instead of a fast mail, an ordinary old post wagon departed, and it was the last one—the next time it would be an express wagon—I had to endure that last one; my hope of still going to Eisenach on Sunday could therefore not be fulfilled; I had to spend the night in Cassel, where we arrived only in the afternoon, rested, went to the theater for half an hour—Goethe’s Egmont—and only yesterday, on Monday, drove to Eisenach with a hired coachman—through forest valleys, a country not exactly pleasant. What we saw of Westphalia, the Wupper valley, then other valleys, the area around Arnsberg was more charming. Here I was no longer in France nor in the beautiful Netherlands, neither as to the regions nor the inns; the latter I noticed because of the good appetite I have; partly because for a few days there have been no good ones to be had, and partly because the coachmen led me to those that in their opinion or according to their interest were good, i.e., bad. I spent the night in Eisenach; in the morning before daybreak, so that I saw nothing of the town (for I had arrived at night), I drove out with a single-horse carriage in thick fog, which was only conquered by the sun towards Gotha; now it went in fine weather, from friendly Gotha to Erfurt, where I sought out Mr. v. Griesheim, but did not find him, though I met his brother, and paid my compliments to his mother, a truly dear, cultivated, and intelligent lady, who was not unknown to me. In the evening—with the setting sun—I then arrived here yesterday. So, after some arranging, I proceeded to the goal of this detour—the old revered friend. The house was illuminated; the Grand Duke had announced himself for tea; however, I had my arrival reported for the time being. Goethe received me in the friendliest and most heartfelt manner; I had many things to tell him; after half an hour the old Grand Duke came;—but I must still add a main point—that I found Zelter with Goethe besides Riemer. Goethe presented me to the gracious Lord, to whom I set myself on the sofa—I believe I even sat to his right—he asked about Paris—he is somewhat deaf. So the evening passed (Zelter and Riemer wisely sat in the adjoining room) as well as it could with the old gentleman, in conversation, until half past ten o’clock. Goethe stood by the whole time; I gradually noticed that the gentleman was somewhat deaf, and that when it became quiet with speaking, one should not try to entertain him, but wait until something occurs to him again—otherwise everything went quite unembarrassed; I had to endure being nailed to my sofa for a couple of hours. The Grand Duke had recommended that I see his botanical garden in Belvedere; I drove with Zelter this morning—Goethe had had his carriage ready for it—at ten o’clock out; they are in fact very large, extensive grounds; the Duke is himself a great botanist—there are beautiful specimens of plants to be seen there—we two were of course not connoisseurs enough to properly appreciate everything—we were back here at noon; I paid my visit to Mr. and Mrs. v. Schwendler, where I naturally heard much regret that you are not there and that I am separated from Goethe in

card: Hegel was at table in Brussels with Mr. van Ghert, his wife and their six children, five boys and one girl; the eldest son was 17. The van Gherts sent their regards to Marie and let Hegel promise that they might come to Berlin in perhaps four years; the eldest son was to complete his studies in Berlin.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I have just left the van Ghert house, where I sat at table with six children—five boys, one girl. The eldest, seventeen, is to come to Berlin in four years to complete his studies. They sent their warmest regards to you; I promised them the door would be open. A fine, bustling family. The wine was passable, though the roast beef was a trifle dry. I paid the usual modest sum for the evening’s hospitality.

I walked back through the dark streets, thinking how strange it is to be a guest in another’s domestic sphere, observing the quiet machinery of a household while the world turns outside. It reminds one that the state is not merely an abstraction but a web of such particular lives.

I am tired but content. The air here is cool. Do tell Karl I saw a boy who might do well with his geometry.

Your affectionate
G.W.F. Hegel
Y: Farewell — in 4 years perhaps we shall see Mr. v. Gh. and his wife in Berlin, who have asked us to recommend them to you in the best possible way, and to grant us the permission to make that promise; we are sitting at the table with 6 children, 5 boys and 1 girl; the eldest son is 17 years old, — when he has completed his studies here, he is to complete them in Berlin, in reliance on us.

card: Hegel and Mr. van Ghert spent four morning hours on foot in Antwerp. Its churches, like Ghent's, hold life-size marble statues; one church can contain two to three dozen large paintings by Rubens, van Dyck and their pupils. There the two parted: van Ghert returned to Brussels to ask after letters from Marie and send them to Amsterdam.
X:
My dearest Marie,

We walked four hours in Antwerp this morning with Mr. van Ghert. The churches are packed with life-size marble statues, and one nave held two dozen large paintings by Rubens and van Dyck. I confess the sheer volume was dizzying; I felt less like a student of history and more like a man drowning in oil paint. Van Ghert returned to Brussels to check for your letters and send them to Amsterdam. I hope they are safe.

I am tired, but the air is fine. I do not know what to write about the food, but the wine was decent. I miss your company and the quiet of our rooms in Berlin. The Dutch are polite, but they lack a certain spark. I shall wait for word. Give my love to the boys.

Your husband,
G.W.F.
Y: Finally, the churches were the subject of conversation. The churches, as I said—in Ghent and Antwerp, one must go there if one wishes to see sublime, rich Catholic churches—large, spacious, Gothic, majestic—stained glass windows (the most beautiful I have ever seen are in Brussels); on the columns, marble statues life-sized, placed at some height, otherwise lying or sitting—in the dozens;—paintings by Rubens, van Dyck, and their pupils, large works, wonderful ones among them, two to three dozen in a single church; marble columns, bas-reliefs, grilles, confessionals, half a dozen or a full dozen in the Antwerp church—each adorned with four life-sized, excellent wood-carved images—(I thought of the English greeting in Nuremberg);—the town halls equally peculiarly Gothic. We were on our feet in Antwerp for four hours in the morning;—I have sweated a lot for the past eight days; at Waterloo I thought that it had not been quite as much as the French and the Allies had sweated. In Antwerp I parted from my dear friend Mr. van Ghert; he went back to Brussels with the instruction to inquire whether any letters from you had arrived, and to send them to me in Amsterdam.

card: Hegel's plan to hire a coachman in Magdeburg with the Englishman fell through, so the two left by diligence at noon the day before, in a coach upholstered and lined with green morocco, and reached Brunswick about 5 am. There they saw the museum, chiefly its picture gallery, including the painting Government Plenipotentiary Schulz had mentioned to Hegel.
X: But now to the matter. So the arrangement with the Englishman to take a hired coach from Magdeburg here has come to nothing; so we set out on the diligence in Magdeburg on Monday noon — to Brunswick. This route to Cassel is the most common, only one or two miles longer than the one I had in mind as the most direct, — has excellent country roads everywhere and good post coaches; and here I must make amends to the Prussian postal service, against which I was indignant in the last letter because of the other routes; the coach is upholstered, lined with green morocco leather, and so forth. Around 5 o'clock in the morning on Tuesday we arrived in Brunswick. — When the suggestion to go via Brunswick was made, it had occurred to me anyway that Mr. Government Commissioner Schulz had told me about a painting that is located there, and which alone is worth a journey. — We have therefore seen the local museum, especially the painting gallery and therein entirely distinguished and outstanding pieces. The painting that Mr. Government Commissioner had in mind is particularly of entirely peculiar excellence.
Y:
My dearest Marie,

We are in Brunswick, having arrived at five this morning after a diligence ride from Magdeburg. The Englishman proved useless; our hired coachman vanished, so we were forced into a green-morocco diligence. It was stifling, but the pace was good.

We visited the museum this morning. The picture gallery is decent, though I must admit I was only looking for the specific painting Schulz mentioned. It is there, and it is merely competent. I paid two thalers for a mediocre lunch; the meat was dry.

I think of Karl and Immanuel. I hope they are well. I will try to find a better coach for the next leg. The heat here is oppressive.

Yours,
Hegel

card: Hegel boarded the diligence again at 3 p.m. the day before and reached Brussels at 6 a.m. He went to bed, had breakfast, received Marie's letter and wrote back at once, and was about to go out with his friend Cousin. He was to leave for Cologne the next morning, where he expected a letter from her.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I write from my room in Brussels, having just finished dinner. The food was competent, if lacking the warmth of home, and I paid four francs for the meal, which I consider fair given the service. I spent the morning resting after the diligence, which was a wretched affair; the driver drove as if he were fleeing a ghost, and my back is still complaining.

I met Cousin this afternoon. He is as lively as ever, though his talk of philosophy grew tedious after the first hour. We walked the streets and looked at the shops. I must confess, the tailors here are inferior to those in Berlin, but I found a decent cravat.

I depart for Cologne tomorrow morning. Do ensure my letter regarding the accounts is waiting for me there, as I need to settle the matter with the publisher. I hope the journey will be less turbulent.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F.
Y: Yesterday afternoon at 3 o’clock I got back into the coach, on which I arrived here this morning at 6 o’clock, then went to bed, had breakfast, and, upon receiving your letter, wrote quickly, in order now to go out with my dear friend and cousin. — Tomorrow morning we continue — to Cölln, where I await a letter from you.

card: Hegel arrived in Töplitz on Saturday afternoon and in Dresden the following evening. He went straight to Tiek's, where he found Professor Hinrichs, who was moving to Halle, and Friedrich von Schlegel, though Hegel learned who Schlegel was only after he had left.
X:
My dearest Marie,

I write from Dresden, where I arrived yesterday evening after a tiring day in Töplitz. The journey is tedious, but the company here is better. I took dinner at Tiek’s and found myself in conversation with Professor Hinrichs, who is moving to Halle. He speaks well, but one senses the restlessness of a man uprooting himself. He left before I could ask him about the new chair, and I suspect he is more interested in his own departure than in the position.

Schlegel was there as well. I did not know who he was until after he had gone. I heard he is a man of some reputation in the Romantic circle, but I confess I have little patience for those who turn philosophy into poetry. It is a pleasant confusion, I suppose, to meet a famous name only to realize you have missed the man.

The food was decent, the wine passable. I paid too much for the room, as is my custom. I hope the boys are well and that Ludwig is not causing trouble. I shall continue on to Vienna in a few days.

Yours,
G.W.F.
Y: P.S. Dresden, October 11, 1824. Arrived in Töplitz on Saturday afternoon, and from there came here yesterday evening — so far, or rather so near, am I to you, my dearest. Last evening I went immediately to Tiek’s and there encountered Professor Hinrichs in the midst of his move to Halle, along with Mr. Friedrich von Schlegel, who was only introduced to me after he had left.

card: Hegel travelled via Abersau and Culm to Töplitz and lodged at a new inn with the sign of the King of Prussia. He then climbed the Schlackenberg opposite the inn, as Fräulein Stok had recommended, drank the waters in the Spitalgarten, walked in the park of Prince Clary's castle, bathed in the Steinbad and dined.
X: Order, and they also want nothing better than that one gets along with them in order. From here it goes over Abersau), Culm — the region of the Battle of Culm, through nothing but a succession of hills and fields — all cultivated and fertile — to Töplitz, which lies very beautifully and pleasantly. I lodged in a brand-new inn (one), because its sign is to the King of Prussia. — Today immediately to the Schlackenberg, which is opposite the inn, — Miss Stok had also recommended this route to me, — on this hill one overlooks the entire region around Töplitz, i.e. if one goes around the top of the hill; — an extremely pleasant view, — the very wide region — finally bounded by higher mountain ranges, — the most varied succession of hills, valleys, rows of houses — everything is most cheerful; — then drank the spring water in the hospital garden — one spring is eye-water, which did me great good — into the park, which belongs to the palace of Prince Clary, the lord of the region — then took a bath in the stone bath — a magnificent spring — then dined with appetite — I shall drive to the castle hill. —
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The road from Abersau was tedious, but Töplitz is a strange place. I lodged at the *König von Preussen*, a new house, and the room is cool, which I prefer to the stifling heat of the spa. I climbed the Schlackenberg as Fräulein Stok advised; the view is adequate, the air sharp. I drank the waters in the Spitalgarten—they taste of iron and regret, but I swallowed them for the sake of the routine. Later, I strolled Prince Clary’s park, which is overgrown and lacks the discipline of a Berlin garden, and took the Steinbad. It was hot, as stones are.

Dinner was serviceable. A roast duck, heavy but acceptable, and a local white wine that lacked backbone. I paid twelve kreuzer for a glass. The people here are polite but shallow, all talking of cures and carriage rides. I think of you and the boys in the quiet of the evening. The world outside is loud, but here, in the water, one’s thoughts settle. I shall write again soon.

Your husband,
G.W.F.

card: From the Schloßberg Hegel viewed the Töplitz basin, 3 to 4 hours wide, between the mountains dividing Saxony from Bohemia and a second range to the south, with the Nollendorf church, Kulm, Marienschein and Aussig on the Elbe. He then walked around Töplitz and saw a few acts of Preciosa at the theatre.
X:
My dearest Marie,

The Töplitz basin, some three hours wide, stretched out before me today from the Schloßberg, a vast amphitheater between the Saxon and Bohemian ranges. Kulm and Marienschein sat quietly on the horizon, with Aussig far off on the Elbe. The air is sharp here, cutting away the Berlin damp.

I strolled the town and, after a modest dinner of roast duck and local wine, attended a performance of *Preciosa*. The acting was wooden, the costumes threadbare; I paid two florins for the privilege of watching talent struggle against its own limitations. I found the audience, however, far more interesting than the stage, their faces reflecting a local pride that seems well-founded in their geography.

Karl’s last letter mentioned the autumn leaves; I see no such romance here, only the clear, cold logic of the mountains. I miss your snuff.

Your G.W.F.
Y: Willdros, in the evening, and specifically Sunday evening). To continue the account! From the Castle Hill there is a view over the entire valley of Töplitz — a valley between two mountain ranges — one being the mountains that separate Saxony from Bohemia, and a second range to the south of it, between which lies a valley three to four hours wide — Töplitz in the middle — the Nollendorf Church on the height, Kulm, Marienschein (you are meant by this), at the foot of the first range — Aussig lies in the corner by the Elbe, between the range towards the east — (the boys should look at the map of the Seven Years' War). Then I still took a walk around Töplitz — finally went to the theatre, a few acts of Preciosa — an even more delicate Zierlisel than the one you so titled in Berlin.

card: Hegel revisited Prince Lichtenstein's gallery until 12 o'clock, then went to Währing, almost half an hour away, to look up Rembold, the local professor of philosophy. He crossed an arm of the Danube to lunch in the Augarten, walked through the Prater, and finished at the Leopoldstadt theatre, where Schuster played a Magister, followed by Die Zauberbirn.
X: At present I still feel yesterday in my bones, for it was a day of hard marching. — After the writing lesson I had with you — I mean, without having first called on you, I could not go out — I went first once more to the Princely Liechtenstein Gallery; — if I were to go there ten more times, I would not exhaust its treasures; — stood in it until 12 o'clock, — then to Währing, — that gallery is nearly half an hour away, — from there, — to visit my colleague, the Professor of the local Chair of Philosophy, Rembold — not as old as I am, a proper fellow countryman of mine, to whom my writings are not unknown), — only the people here] all stay too much cooped up, — traveling and getting about does not come so easily to them as to us. — From there I crossed a branch of the Danube and went to the Augarten for lunch, — never so tasty and so cheap as in my inn, where the fatal carriage meal takes place, and ate with a good appetite; afterwards I looked around in the Augarten. The garden is maintained just like the one in Schönbrunn, — broad, grand avenues, — the trees, shrubs in the paths cut into vertical flat walls, the trees like fans, or as if you left the stem on a pear and cut it into a disc on it, about as thick as the stem is, — so that one walks only between trees, not under trees and foliage, and always has the sky, which today was indeed so beautifully blue, above one's head; also the sun is already lower, so there is shade from the walls. — But at the end of the Augarten there is a view of the richest countryside, which has the hills about an hour away — Leopoldsberg, Kahlenberg — as its boundary, — in the most beautiful light the most beautiful landscape! — For such spots we are to be envied here. — Afterwards to the Prater — a forest, as I love it, with green grass, without any undergrowth and bushes between the tree trunks; — besides an innumerable number of taverns, bowling greens, carousels, optical room travels etc., I found some very elegant coffee pavilions here one writes correctly Kaffeh) — finally, after long wandering about, out of fatigue, to rest, to the Leopoldstadt Theatre, where Schuster played a Magister quite excellently, otherwise spoke High German; the second was again the Magic Pear, and went, very tired, in the most beautiful moonlight, — the fine weather is unchangeably faithful — home and to supper
Y:
My dearest Marie,

The heat in Vienna is a trial. I spent the morning at Prince Lichtenstein’s gallery until noon, where the light was better than the crowd. Then I took the carriage to Währing, half an hour out, to see Rembold. He is a decent man, though his philosophy is mostly dust. We crossed the Danube arm to lunch in the Augarten. The fish was acceptable, costing me two florins, but the wine was thin.

I walked the Prater, which is merely trees and noise, then caught the Leopoldstadt theatre. Schuster played the Magister; he is loud and wooden. The farce, *Die Zauberbirn*, followed. It was vulgar, but the audience loved it. I paid a gulden for the seat.

Karl’s letter arrived yesterday; he is well, though his arithmetic remains slow. I shall send the books I promised when I return.

Your affectionate,
G.W.F.
